newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Astra shareholders say no changes likely.
newsitem.headline: Astra shareholders say no changes likely.

text.p: Five top Indonesian businessmen, confirming they own more than half the shares in the country's largest car maker, Astra Internasional, have said they do not plan management changes, news reports said on Wednesday.
"The synergy of the company is already good so why should we change anything," timber tycoon Muhamad "Bob" Hasan was quoted as saying in the Kompas daily.
"There may be some nuts and bolts that need tightening...but we don't have to change the engine," Hasan said.

The chief executive of the Salim Group, Anthony Salim, was quoted in Bisnis Indonesia daily as saying the shareholders believed in the future of Astra and wanted to increase investment in the company.
"The point is that we want to increase investment. Therefore it is not true that we have our own hidden agendas about Astra," Salim said.
The pair met with reporters on Tuesday.

Hasan is head of the Nusamba group that holds a 10 percent stake in Astra. Nusamba is 80 percent owned by three charitable foundations headed by President Suharto. Hasan and the president's eldest son Sigit Hardjojudanto each own 10 percent.
The Salim group, which holds around an 11 percent stake, is controlled by Liem Sioe Liong, believed to be Indonesia's wealthiest man and a close associate of Suharto.

The meeting with reporters also was attended by Putera Sampoerna, head of cigarette manufacturer PT Handala Manjaya Sampoerna, Prajogo Pangestu of PT Delta Mustika and Usman Admadjaja of Danamon Internasional, which controls Bank Danamon.
Sampoerna holds 15 percent of Astra, making him the largest single shareholder.
The meeting comes after months of speculation about Astra. Sampoerna bought heavily into the company in September and October, triggering speculation he was attempting a takeover.
Brokers have said subsequent buying by the other four members at the meeting may have been an effort to block him.
In total, the five businessmen hold more than 50 percent of the shares in the widely-held Astra, in which Toyota Motor Co of Japan has an 8.26 percent stake.
Suharto said last week that no single stakeholder should control more than 15 percent of any listed company. It was not immediately clear whether the president was referring to Astra.
